summary:
Section 377 of the Penal Code of 1861, enacted in 1886, criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. It prohibits carnal intercourse with any man, woman or animal and provides for imprisonment ranging between life and a term of not less than two years, extendable to ten years, with a fine of between 400 and 1,000 rupees. The prohibition applies regardless of consent or privacy and reaches heterosexual anal and oral sex as well. Enforcement has been described as inconsistent, but the provision remains in active use: in November 2018 the HIV-positive advocate Aung Myo Htut, also known as Addy Chen, was charged under it in Yangon over an alleged offence against an employee.

A June 2024 submission by Human Rights Myanmar to the UN Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial executions reports that section 377 enforcement has intensified since the coup of 1 February 2021, operating as an aggravating factor alongside militarised policing, arbitrary detention and vaguely worded public-decency provisions that endanger the right to life. The same submission documents the killing of between 5 and 12 LGBTIQ+ persons in military-controlled Myanmar since the coup. The National Unity Government recorded 17 LGBT people killed and 2 critically injured between 1 February 2021 and January 2024, according to DVB. These are raw counts without a population denominator and do not by themselves establish a per-capita rate.

Section 35(c) of the Police Act of 1945, described as the 'shadow law' or 'darkness law', permits police to detain anyone considered to be behaving suspiciously after sunset, for up to three months; it is used specifically against transgender people. Other Penal Code provisions cited as usable against LGBTQ people include sections 269 and 270 (negligently spreading a sexually transmitted disease), section 290 (public nuisance, fines up to 200 rupees), sections 292, 293 and 294 ('obscene' material, songs or public acts), section 372 (buying or selling a prostitute under eighteen), section 469 (marriage ceremony absent legal marriage), and section 5(j) of the Emergency Provisions Act (anything affecting morality negatively).

Myanmar does not allow transgender people to change the gender assigned to them at birth, and the state does not recognise their gender identity; no legal gender recognition procedure or documentary process exists. Transgender people are subject to police harassment, sexual assault including rape, mistreatment and extortion. Documented instances include a 2013 case in Mandalay where trans women were forced to strip and parade naked while photographed, with police calling it a 'public service', and the account of trans woman Nat Nat We, who described arrest, stripping, a beating and 14 days' detention for walking home at night in a case where police accused her of sex work (reported 2016). Trans women are frequently denied equal access to professions, overrepresented in spirit mediums and sex work.

Myanmar does not recognise same-sex marriages or civil unions. Ceremonial marriages and cohabitation carry no legal standing. A 2014 unofficial wedding by a same-sex couple together for ten years triggered a backlash from social conservatives questioning why anti-homosexuality laws were not enforced against them.

There are no enforceable legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity. The 2019 Child Rights Law contains a non-discrimination clause referencing sexual orientation but applies only to children and lacks enforcement mechanisms. The 2020 MRTV Broadcasting Guidelines discourage discriminatory media portrayals but carry no legal penalties. The 2022 Gender Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights includes LGBTQ individuals as a vulnerable group in healthcare delivery, but it is a planning document rather than an enforceable law.

Outright International's overview (updated March 2026) reports that section 377 is used to detain people who cannot 'satisfactorily account' for their presence, and that risks intensified after the coup of 1 February 2021: torture and sexual violence in detention; the Organization Registration Law of October 2022, which provides prison terms for NGO non-compliance; compulsory military service announced in February 2024; and seven LGBTQ-themed books banned in 2025. Its verdict for LGBT travellers is to avoid the country entirely. In January 2025 Radio Free Asia reported that the junta banned seven named LGBTQ-themed books as 'obscene' and announced prosecutions for publishers.

The ASEAN SOGIE Caucus reported in March 2025, drawing on research by Queers of Burma Alternative from January 2025, that the 2024 Conscription Law drives queer people into fear and displacement. A survey cited by DVB in January 2024, 'Rainbow Amid the Storm', found that 50% of LGBT respondents had no confidence in the legal system and over 68% feared repercussions from abusers; the source does not state the survey's field period.

Section 377 was called out by Aung San Suu Kyi in 2013 as hampering the country's efforts to combat HIV, and gay men are stigmatised, especially if living with HIV/AIDS. Following the June 2019 death by suicide of young gay librarian Kyaw Zin Win after workplace harassment at Myanmar Imperial University in Yangon, the university opened an investigation and suspended three staff members, and the Myanmar National Human Rights Commission called for enactment of anti-discrimination provisions.

Nat kadaws (spirit mediums) are culturally visible transgender women, and as a nat kadaw a transgender Burmese person can be afforded respect and veneration otherwise denied by society; 'Occult' is a local term for the transgender community. A 2020 poll found 74% agreed being LGBTQ should be legal (23% disagreed) and 81% agreed that LGBT people deserve equal treatment (12% disagreed). Social mores about human sexuality have been described as extremely conservative, and in local Buddhist tradition those born LGBTQ are perceived as facing punishment for sins committed in a past life.

outOfScopeNotes:
The field period for the 'Rainbow Amid the Storm' survey cited by DVB in January 2024 is not stated in the source, so the 50% and 68% figures cannot be dated to a specific window.

The killing figures from Human Rights Myanmar (5 to 12 since the coup, June 2024) and the National Unity Government (17 killed, 2 critically injured, reported January 2024) are raw counts without population denominators; no per-capita comparison to Myanmar's general homicide rate is available in this inventory, so the trans-specific magnitude above background violence is unresolved.

Outright International's 'avoid entirely' verdict is the source's own assessment, not a finding of this record.
